opening.headline: When the AI tools used by each department are different, the company determines by what criteria to divide the construction of enterprise apps and APIs themselves.
body: Let's say the legal team uses a tool to summarize contracts, the development team uses a tool for code assistance and model calls, and the marketing team uses a free chatbot for their personal accounts. Each person made a reasonable choice, but when looking at the organization as a whole, it is not possible to see at a glance who uses what tools, who pays the costs, and whether access to those who have left the company is blocked.

In this lesson, we first see that an enterprise app is a device that manages members, permissions, seating, and analytics in one place, rather than the model itself. We then look at ways to automate the account lifecycle and role-based access control, compared to the path of building your own API by calling models in code. Lastly, we set a standard for judgment by analyzing the demands of the legal team and the development team through examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise, Gemini Enterprise and API construction
You can divide the department's needs into those that can be resolved through enterprise apps and those that can be resolved through self-construction, and present the rationale.
It is possible to distinguish and explain which layer of the authentication and account life cycle IdP, SSO, and SCIM are each responsible for.

items.prompt: Legal: Document summarization tool for contract review
items.answer: The legal team subscribed to a separate document summary tool to quickly review contracts. Although it is helpful for work, enterprise administrators do not know which accounts and settings handle sensitive documents such as contracts. Even if the person using this tool leaves the company, there is no separate procedure to terminate access.

items.prompt: Development team: code assistance and calling your own model
items.answer: The development team uses code assistance tools and creates a separate development account to directly call the model API. Interactive app payments and API payments are managed in different systems, so costs from the same team are billed in two places.

items.prompt: Marketing Team: Free chatbot for personal account
items.answer: Each marketing team uses a free chatbot with their own personal account. Because the organization did not create the account, the organization cannot reclaim the account and there is no way to check what data was pasted. This is the least noticeable, yet most difficult to control example.

items.prompt: HR: Who organizes access to all of this?
items.answer: The HR team has information on joining and leaving the company, but there is no way to follow and organize the accounts of tools scattered across departments. All three risks - duplicate payments, personal accounts, and unauthorized sharing - stem from one fact: tools are scattered.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified what the confusion looks like, let's start by recalling similar experiences.

screens.title: Think about it: Our organization's tool landscape
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to type or submit your answer, so just think of it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Each department uses different tools. How do you organize it in transcription? Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: In most organizations, tools are created first by the department that needs them, and organization comes later. At this time, the starting point for organizing is not the list of tools, but the question, ‘Who uses them and with what authority?’ This lesson will focus on the management functions that answer that question.

items.prompt: Who created the account and who canceled it then?
items.answer: It is rare for the person who created the account to cancel the account. If the person creating it and the person canceling it are different, it is easy for cancellation to be missed. So enterprise products provide a way to leave the creation and release of accounts to the organization's identity system rather than to human memory.

items.prompt: When a person leaves the company, what happens to their access rights?
items.answer: If it's a personal account, your organization can't do anything, and even if it's an organization account, you might miss out if you rely on manual deletion. The first criterion for selecting a corporate product is whether the resignation process automatically follows the deassignment of the identity system.

items.prompt: Did you know whose budget the costs were coming from?
items.answer: Interactive apps are often billed per seat and APIs are often billed per usage, so you'll see the two costs on different screens. The OpenAI document also explains that the payment systems of ChatGPT and the API platform are separate. Knowing your cost structure is also part of organizing your tools.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's see what makes enterprise apps different from personal apps.

labels: Created by yourself and managed by yourself

states.label: personal account
states.body: You create a personal account, make payments yourself, and set your own settings. Your organization won't know who is on this account, what features they have turned on, or how much it costs. It's convenient for users, but from an organization's perspective, there's no way to cut off access or enforce policies.

states.label: Workspace (for businesses)
states.body: The core of an enterprise app is the management screen, not the model. In ChatGPT Enterprise, Workspace settings is the main management screen, where owners and administrators handle membership, seat defaults, feature access, GPT governance, apps, analytics, and identity controls based on their role. Workspace settings are visible to all roles, but company-wide settings such as permissions, seat types, spend controls, and feature access are set by owners and administrators. You can also place your organization's AI policy notice in your workspace. If you turn the policy on, users will see the notice every 30 days and again if you change the content. Licenses are assigned and retrieved on a per-seat basis, and the roles that can manage them are limited.

screens.outro: Now that we have the concept of a workspace, let's look at how to bring people in and out.

screens.title: Identity Provider (IdP), SSO, SCIM: Login and account lifecycle are different layers
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the process of changing from creating separate accounts for each service to having a single identity provider. In the final step, we note that login and account lifecycle are different layers.

visual.alt: A schematic diagram depicting the flow in which the identity provider delivers login assurance to the service and the flow in which account creation and cancellation are delivered as two different arrows.
labels: Identity Provider (IdP): Check member list and logins
Deliver login assurance: SAML or OpenID Connect (SSO)

steps.title: When each service has a separate account
steps.body: Every time a service is added, the user creates a new ID and password, and the service keeps a separate user list within itself. From an organization's perspective, when joining the company, you must create as many accounts as there are services, and when you leave the company, you must delete as many accounts as there are services. If you leave out even one part, the account of the person who left the company will remain. To solve this problem, we need to determine 'who this person is' in one place.

steps.title: IdP: Guarantee ‘who you are’ in one place
steps.body: An IdP (Identity Provider) is a system that manages the identity of organization members and verifies logins. The service does not directly verify the user's password, but trusts and accepts the result as assured by the IdP that 'this person is authenticated'. The reason a service can trust an IdP is because a trust relationship has been established in advance between the two, and this relationship is usually confirmed by cryptographic means such as a certificate. In this way, the service leaves the login decision to the IdP and focuses on its own work.

steps.title: SSO: Protocol for delivering assurance results to services
steps.body: SSO (Single Sign-On) is a method that allows multiple services to accept the results of one login, and the representative protocols for delivering assurance results are SAML and OpenID Connect. The flow is similar. When a user accesses the service, the service sends the browser to the IdP, the IdP verifies the login, sends the signed result back to the service, and the service verifies the signature and lets the user in. SAML 2.0 contains the authentication fact in an XML-based assertion, and OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 and contains the authentication result in an ID token (JWT). What this step conveys is that you know who this person is and that you are verified, and it does not involve creating or deleting an account.

steps.title: SCIM: Protocol for communicating account creation, modification, and cancellation
steps.body: System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) is an HTTP-based protocol for provisioning and managing identity data. For the Users and Groups resources exposed by the service, the IdP operates by sending a POST request for creation, PUT or PATCH for change, and DELETE request for deletion. The appearance of user properties is determined by the SCIM Core Schema, a separate standard. So, when a new employee is assigned to an app by the IdP, a user is created in the service, and when a former employee is assigned, the service account is deactivated or deleted. This process occurs regardless of whether the user is logged in or not.

steps.title: What you see when you divide the two floors
steps.body: To summarize, SSO is the authentication layer and SCIM is the account lifecycle layer. Even if authentication is automated based on the IdP, if people are responsible for creating and deleting accounts within the service, the two layers are misaligned. For example, even if a person who leaves the company is no longer authenticated by the IdP, account items may remain in the service, occupy seats, and remain visible on the management screen. So the next screen compares when an account was created by method. These two layers explain why the judgment that ‘since SSO is turned on, account management is automatic’ is incorrect.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that login and account lifecycles are different layers, let's compare the different methods for when accounts are created and released.

screens.title: People and Authority: SSO, JIT, SCIM
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare when an account is created and how it is released when you leave the company.

visual.alt: Schematic showing the flow from IdP to service and three provisioning methods.
labels: SCIM (synchronizes assignment changes from account creation to account cancellation)

tabs.label: SSO first
tabs.body: SSO and domain verification must be completed before choosing a provisioning method. Claude's setup guide also sets out the order to select a user provisioning method after completing SSO and linking with the IdP. SSO is an authentication method that determines how people log in, and creating and deleting accounts is handled by a separate provisioning method. If you consider the two as the same, you will end up with a situation where authentication is automatic but account deactivation is manual.

tabs.label: Invite only
tabs.body: Invite only is the default. Administrators can add and delete members directly from the settings screen, and also change roles and seat types. It is good because it is simple for small organizations or pilot introductions, but as the number of people increases, the risk of missing the release of retired employees increases.

tabs.label: JIT
tabs.body: Just-in-time (JIT) is a method in which accounts are automatically created when users assigned to an IdP's app log in for the first time. New employees can use it right away without any manual work from the administrator. However, since the user's first login is when an account is created, changes that occur while not logged in are not synchronized. Claude is available for Team plan, Enterprise plan, and Console organizations.

tabs.label: SCIM
tabs.body: SCIM directory synchronization creates and releases users based on assignment changes from the IdP. It works even before the user logs in, so the exiting user's access disappears when the IdP de-assigns it. In Claude, SCIM can only be used in Enterprise plan and Console organizations, but not in Team plan. OpenAI also notes that SCIM synchronizes users and groups with your IdP, and that SCIM is not included in the standalone ChatGPT Business plan.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the lifecycle of an account, let's move on to role-based controls that further refine access to features.

screens.title: RBAC splits functional access
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, a short explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: ChatGPT's role-based access control (RBAC) configures feature access through a reusable custom role. Members can receive roles directly or through group membership and may hold multiple roles. Member, Admin, and Owner are built-in roles that determine what a person may manage; a custom role determines which features they may use. Each permission has three states: default, on, or off. Permissions from multiple roles use additive combination, so a member retains access if any role grants it. In NIST's RBAC model, permissions are attached to roles rather than directly to users, who obtain permissions through their assigned roles. As roles accumulate, a person's total access can exceed what was intended. Design roles according to least privilege and review them regularly. Only workspace Owners may create and assign a custom role; Admins are limited to viewing or updating existing roles. Claude also offers a custom role and Spending limits per group on its Enterprise plan.

terms.tip: A reusable role that determines what functionality can be used. Only the workspace owner is responsible for creating and assigning.
These are roles that exist from the beginning, such as Member, Admin, and Owner. It determines how much of the workspace can be managed, not access to features.
This means that when the permissions of multiple roles are combined, access is maintained if even one is allowed. Even if you turn it off in one role, it won't be blocked if another role allows it.
Claude Enterprise has the ability to set spending caps on a group basis. It is used for departmental cost control.
It is a security principle that provides only the access necessary for work. The AC-6 controls in NIST SP 800-53 address this principle. It serves as a standard for designing and checking roles.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Reading legal team requests into an enterprise app
screens.lead: The instructor explains the legal team's needs step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Putting Requests Into Sentences
steps.body: The legal team has four demands. You want to summarize the contract, the contract should not leave the organization, access should be blocked immediately to those who leave the company, and records of usage should be maintained for audit purposes. Of these, only the first is directly related to the performance of the model. The remaining three are all requests for management capabilities.

steps.title: Check out the identity life cycle first
steps.body: Before comparing model performance, let's see whether SSO and SCIM can automate the identity lifecycle. This is because in order to immediately block access of employees who have left the company, de-assignment of the IdP must lead to account deactivation. SCIM syncs regardless of whether you're logged in or not, but Claude is only available on the Enterprise line, so your choice of plan will determine whether it meets your needs.

steps.title: Open only the features you need
steps.body: Create a custom role just for legal, opening only the features needed for contract summaries and not the rest. Because role privileges are combined in an additive manner, it is important to ensure that legal members do not also have other roles to maintain the intended scope.

steps.title: Check with policy and analysis
steps.body: Inform members of the usage principles through the workspace's AI policy notice, and see if usage status can be checked through the analysis screen. Usage history is audit-on-demand, and what records you can see and for what period of time may vary depending on your plan, so it's a good idea to list out what you need in advance.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: The legal team's needs are met with administrative functionality without writing a single line of code. So enterprise apps are a good fit. The basis for the judgment was not the superiority or inferiority of the model, but that most of the needs were in the management functions of identity, authority, policy, and analysis.

screens.outro: Let’s use the same framework to solve development team demands of opposite nature.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Why API is the development team's request?
screens.lead: This time, we will address the development team’s needs step by step. Select the right arrow to follow how the decision is narrowed down.

steps.title: read request
steps.body: Development teams want to put model calls into in-house services, view costs on a per-call basis, and tie them into cloud contracts they already have in place. This is a request that a program calls a model, rather than something a person writes in a dialog box.

steps.title: Is it screen or code?
steps.body: First, decide whether you need a conversation screen or a code call. If it needs to be called automatically within the service, it cannot be resolved through the app's management screen and an API path is required. This is the same reason why the OpenAI document describes ChatGPT and the payment system of the API platform separately.

steps.title: Fit to the cloud you already use
steps.body: If you already have a cloud in use, it is easier to organize by following that cloud's authentication and payment path. If you use AWS, Claude Platform on AWS authenticates with AWS IAM and payment is made through AWS Marketplace, and Bedrock is billed for AWS service usage.

steps.title: Check functions and names
steps.body: The timing of feature provision and service name varies from cloud to cloud. The Bedrock path follows the Bedrock release schedule for feature availability and does not support Agent Skills. Google renamed Vertex AI to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. You should first check whether the features you need are in the path you choose.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Legal affairs is divided into corporate apps, and development is divided into APIs. Instead, the standards for identity and cost are unified across the company. The common conclusion drawn from both cases is to divide the tools but combine the management framework.

screens.outro: Combining the two cases, the question remains: how many vendors will there be?

screens.title: Commentary 3: Weighing the pros and cons of multi-vendor
screens.lead: Use the slider to vary the number of vendors you use to see how your choice and management burden change.

visual.alt: A diagram that places the advantages and management burdens of multi-vendor on both sides of a scale.
labels: Select the optimal model for each task

stops.body: It is easiest to unify policies because there is one management screen, role system, and invoice. On the other hand, the entire organization is affected by one company's failure or price change, and the range of choices to choose the right model for each task is narrow. The administrative burden is lowest and the choices are narrowest.

You will be less dependent on one company and can choose a model that better suits your business. Instead, there are two management screens and two invoices, and the same function is provided under different names and conditions for each company, making it necessary to match policies.

It has the widest range of choices, but management items increase as the number of businesses increases. Different role structures and billing formats make it difficult to see company-wide costs at a glance. OpenAI's investment management guidance also considers visibility into who uses which products and models and how much as the first step.

Align identity with one IdP, cost reporting in one format, and delegate model selection to your department. By dividing what needs to be unified and what needs to be entrusted, you can reduce management complexity while maintaining the advantages of multi-vendor.

screens.outro: I will organize the scale's conclusions into a standard table.

screens.title: Key takeaway: What separates enterprise apps from APIs?
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: The core of an enterprise app is not a model, but a device that manages membership, permissions, seating, and analytics in one place. Identity automates the life cycle with JIT or SCIM on top of SSO, and feature access is segmented into custom roles and groups.

If you need to call code, you're building the API itself. At this time, you must confirm that the operating entity, authentication, payment, and function provision timing are different for each route. The app's management screen and the API's payment path are often operated separately.

Multi-vendor reduces dependency risk and increases job-specific choices, but also increases management screens and invoices. So the compromise of unifying identity and cost reporting but delegating model selection is realistic.

When a department request comes up, ask this first. Is this request a problem with the screen a person uses, or a problem with a call made by a program? If it's a screen issue, if the need is a management function, it's a corporate app, if it's a call issue, it's building the API itself. This question alone puts most needs down one of two paths.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Tools are divided according to needs, but the standards for identity and cost are aligned across the company.

data.notes: If the request is a management function, it is sent to the app; if it is a call, it is sent to the API. Organizations that use both paths align identity and cost criteria together.

glossary.def: An administrative unit in which an organization's members, settings, and policies are grouped. It becomes the standard for uniformly applying company-wide policies to all members.
This is a provisioning standard that automatically reflects changes in user assignment from the IdP to the service. Synchronizes account creation and cancellation.
This method automatically creates an account when a user assigned to the IdP app logs in for the first time.
It is a permission model that divides function access into roles. The permissions of multiple roles are combined in an additive manner.
This is the right to allocate and retrieve seats on a per-seat basis. The roles you can manage are limited.

An IdP (Identity Provider) is a system that manages members' identities and guarantees logins. SSO is a method of delivering the guarantee to multiple services using SAML or OpenID Connect and using it with a single login.

misconceptions.myth: When you subscribe to an enterprise app, the API is automatically included.
misconceptions.fact: The app's management screen and the API's payment and authentication path are often operated separately. OpenAI also explains that the payment systems of ChatGPT and the API platform are separate.

misconceptions.myth: SCIM is available on all plans.
misconceptions.fact: In Claude, SCIM can only be used in the Enterprise plan and some Console organizations, and the Team plan includes JIT. OpenAI also does not include SCIM in the standalone Business plan.

The benefits of decentralization come at the cost of increased management screens, role structures, and billing as the number of businesses increases. Failure to unify identity and cost criteria may actually result in less control.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The enterprise app manages members, permissions, seating, and analytics in one place.
Identity lifecycle automation with JIT or SCIM on top of SSO.
If a code call is required, the API itself is built, and the operating entity and payment are different for each route.
Multi-vendor trades choice for choice and management complexity, thus unifying identity and cost criteria.
